title: CNAS Insights | Strategic Stability with China Will Come at a Cost
gist: Kilcrease and Gertz argue the US-China 'strategic stability' framing adopted after the May summit is a US concession forced by China's rare-earth retaliation, and that it will either break down or cost US interests (Taiwan, Iran sanctions, Russia). Their remedy: stop bullying allies and build a coalition of industrial democracies to blunt Chinese geoeconomic leverage.

insights.claim: The US-China 'strategic stability' agreement is best understood as a US concession after China retaliated against last summer's tariffs and export controls, including by restricting rare earth exports.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Signals China's chokepoint leverage works; US less likely to escalate tariffs/controls near term.
insights.quote: The agreement on strategic stability is best understood as a U.S. concession

insights.claim: The strategic stability framing, borrowed from nuclear mutually assured destruction, reflects that each side can inflict severe economic pain on the other, so restraint is mutually beneficial.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Useful lens: economic deterrence equilibrium dampens tail risk of trade war escalation while it holds.
insights.locator: Strategic stability, adopted from Cold War

insights.claim: For Trump strategic stability enables dealmaking, while for Xi it deters the US from using geoeconomic leverage against Beijing's core interests.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Asymmetric objectives make the truce fragile.
insights.locator: Strategic stability, adopted from Cold War

insights.claim: Strategic stability is unlikely to last, and if it does, it will come at a significant cost to US interests.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Investors should expect renewed US-China economic weaponization risk.
insights.quote: But it is unlikely to last—and if it does, it will come at a significant cost to U.S. interests.
insights.locator: Coming out of the previous summit

insights.claim: Since the May summit the US has not added a single Chinese company to the Entity List, signaled a ceiling on tariff rates for China, while China has begun slowly licensing rare earth exports.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Concrete indicators to monitor for truce health: Entity List additions, tariff caps, rare earth licensing pace.
insights.quote: The United States has not added a single Chinese company to its Entity List

insights.claim: Both sides are intensifying decoupling: the US is purging Chinese products from defense supply chains, building non-China rare earth markets, and banning Chinese drones and robotics, while China punishes firms that move supply chains out.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Supports non-China rare earth, defense supply-chain and domestic drone/robotics plays even during the truce; raises risk for firms relocating out of China.
insights.locator: At the same time, both sides

insights.claim: The uneasy compromise lets each side defend its supply chains as long as neither weaponizes economic chokepoints, but there is no shared understanding of when defense tips into weaponization.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Miscalculation risk is high; a defensive measure could trigger a new rare-earth-style shock.
insights.quote: there is no shared understanding of when defensive actions tip into weaponization of economic ties
insights.locator: Strategic stability could also be upended

insights.claim: Taiwan is a likely breaking point: China's stability is contingent on US non-interference, yet failure to respond to escalating coast guard drills would undermine US credibility.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Taiwan escalation is a key tail risk for semis and global markets.

insights.claim: The Iran conflict tests the truce because US officials threaten to punish countries offering Iran economic lifelines, while China, Iran's largest oil buyer, has promised stiff retaliation against sanctions on that trade.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Secondary sanctions on Chinese oil buyers could reignite trade war and affect oil flows.
insights.locator: The ongoing Iran conflict is another test.

insights.claim: China has acted as a sanctions spoiler in most major US campaigns over the last decade, so effective sanctions increasingly require targeting Chinese entities.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Sanctions enforcement and truce maintenance are structurally in conflict.
insights.quote: wielding them effectively increasingly means targeting Chinese entities that undermine them

insights.claim: The authors recommend the US stop bullying allies and coordinate a coalition of advanced industrial democracies large enough to blunt Chinese retaliation and sustain non-China suppliers of critical goods.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: An allied market approach would benefit non-China critical-goods suppliers; absent it, the US is stuck.
insights.quote: The obvious answer to these challenges is to stop bullying U.S. allies
insights.locator: The obvious answer to these challenges
